description: In Word Swap questions, a sentence is provided with certain highlighted words placed in incorrect positions. Candidates must swap these words with each other to make the sentence grammatically correct and contextually meaningful. This topic tests vocabulary, grammar, and reading comprehension skills.

sections.title: Basic Concepts and Question Types
sections.description: This section explains the foundational principles of Word Swap and the standard format of questions asked in exams.

key_concepts.explanation: Identifying whether a highlighted word is a noun, verb, or adjective is crucial. A misplaced word often breaks the grammatical structure of the sentence, making it easy to spot by analyzing its part of speech.
Sometimes a word might fit grammatically but fail to make sense in the overall context of the sentence. Logical understanding is required to ensure the swapped words convey a coherent meaning.

question_types.explanation: A single sentence contains 3 to 5 bold or highlighted words. You need to identify which words have been swapped and choose the correct pair or sequence from the options.
question_types.approach: Read the sentence normally to spot the word that breaks the flow, determine its correct part of speech, and find the appropriate replacement among the other highlighted words.

sections.title: Important Grammar Rules
sections.description: Crucial grammatical rules necessary to ensure structural accuracy while swapping words.

grammar_rules.explanation: A singular subject must be paired with a singular verb, and a plural subject with a plural verb. If a plural subject is followed by a highlighted singular verb, it indicates that a swap is required.
In English, the preposition 'To' is generally followed by the base form of a verb. If 'To' is followed by a highlighted noun or an '-ing' form, swap it with a highlighted V1 verb.
An adjective always describes a noun and typically precedes it. If a verb or an unrelated word is placed just before a noun, it should be swapped with an appropriate adjective.

sections.title: Key Indicators
sections.description: Identifying hidden clues in the sentence that act as strong hints for correctly matching words.

key_indicators.usage_hint: If a highlighted word does not agree with the preposition immediately following it (e.g., 'Interested' followed by 'on'), swap it with a word that naturally takes that preposition.
Conjunctions connect identical grammatical structures. If there is a V-ing verb on one side of 'and', the highlighted word on the other side must also be in the V-ing form.

sections.title: Examples and Explanations
sections.description: This section demonstrates the practical application of concepts through solved examples.

examples.incorrect_or_context: The government has (A) decided to (B) poor free food grains to the (C) distribute.
examples.correct_or_usage: The government has (A) decided to (C) distribute free food grains to the (B) poor.
examples.explanation: The preposition 'to' requires the base verb 'distribute' (C). The article 'the' requires the noun 'poor' (B). Therefore, swapping B and C makes the sentence grammatically correct.

examples.incorrect_or_context: The (A) doctor prescribed some (B) healthy to help the patient stay (C) medicines.
examples.correct_or_usage: The (A) doctor prescribed some (C) medicines to help the patient stay (B) healthy.
examples.explanation: The word 'some' must be followed by a noun, which is 'medicines' (C). The verb 'stay' needs an adjective complement, which is 'healthy' (B). Thus, B and C should be swapped.

sections.title: Strategies to Solve
sections.description: Effective strategies to save time and maximize accuracy during the examination.

strategies.title: Read without Options
strategies.detail: First, read the sentence quickly without looking at the options. Doing this will naturally help you spot the awkward or out-of-place word that breaks the logical flow.

strategies.title: Match Parts of Speech
strategies.detail: If a specific position strictly requires a noun, but holds an adjective, immediately scan the other highlighted words to find the missing noun.

strategies.title: Process of Elimination
strategies.detail: Use the answer choices to your advantage. If you are 100% sure that word (A) must swap with word (C), instantly eliminate all options that do not contain the (A-C) pair.

exceptions.explanation: Sometimes standard grammar rules take a backseat because certain words in English habitually co-occur (collocations). In such cases, you must identify customary word pairings rather than relying solely on parts of speech.
exceptions.example: For instance, 'Make a decision' is correct, whereas 'Do a decision' is wrong, even though both 'make' and 'do' are verbs.
